job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# Drafting Review: S. 2817 (Manager's Amendment, Oct. 6, 2026)

This review is based on the bill text only. Points involving existing statutes (especially DSHMRA) and constitutional questions should be checked with counsel before they go into testimony or talking points.

**Section 2 (Definitions)**

1. **§2(1)(A), single-vessel trigger:** The 10,000-ton threshold applies to "a single vessel," with no aggregation language. An operator using several vessels that each stay under the threshold would fall outside the definition.

2. **§2(1)(A), measurement:** The bill does not say how tonnage is measured (wet or dry weight, nodules recovered or retained, gross or net of sediment, annual average or any twelve-month period). Operators can argue they are below the line under any reasonable method.

3. **§2(1)(A), undefined terms:** "Recovery," "mineral resources," "seabed," and "depths" are undefined. It is unclear whether sediment, crust, or sulfide deposits count, and whether depth is measured at the site or through the water column.

4. **§2(1), "commercial" is undefined:** The heading says "commercial," but the operative text requires no sale, profit, or commercial purpose. It is therefore arguable that test or pilot recovery above the threshold is not "commercial."

5. **§2(1)(B), open-ended Secretary determination:** The Secretary may designate activities as covered if they pose "comparable" risks, with no criteria, procedure, notice, or comment requirement, and no stated standard for review. This invites an APA challenge that could come from either side.

6. **§2(1)(B) and §6, which Secretary:** The bill never defines "the Secretary." §6 refers to the Secretary of State, and §4 implies NOAA (Commerce), so §2(1)(B) is ambiguous.

7. **§2(2), "U.S. person" is narrow:** It covers only citizens and corporations organized under a State's law. It excludes LLCs, partnerships, and project vehicles, and "State" is undefined (territories and D.C. are unclear). Many U.S.-linked entities therefore fall outside §3(a)'s "any U.S. person anywhere" reach.

8. **§2(3), covered vessel:** The 5,000 gross-ton threshold and the phrase "equipped for" are undefined. A vessel under 5,000 GT with capacity to exceed 10,000 tons per year is prohibited under §2(1)(A) but is not a "covered vessel," so it escapes the §4 registry and reporting.

**Section 3 (Prohibition and Exemptions)**

9. **§3(a), "engage in" is undefined:** The prohibition does not clearly reach financing, insurance, equipment supply, vessel chartering, processing, or offtake. Support activities could continue even if the mining itself stops.

10. **§3(a), geographic reach:** "In the United States" is not defined for the seabed. A non-U.S. person operating in the international Area or on the high seas is outside §3(a) entirely, and the bill does not address foreign-flagged vessels operated by U.S.-linked companies.

11. **§3 generally, no trade or possession ban:** Nothing prohibits importing, selling, possessing, or processing minerals recovered in violation of §3. Enforcement against the operator alone would leave a downstream market in place.

12. **§3(b), "exploration license" is undefined and unattached:** The bill does not identify the issuing authority (NOAA under DSHMRA, an International Seabed Authority contract, or a foreign state). This creates ambiguity about which licenses are protected.

13. **§3(b), no limits on grandfathered activity:** The exemption has no cap on volume, area, vessels, duration, or sales. A licensee could expand commercial production substantially while staying within the exemption.

14. **§3(b), pending and renewed licenses:** The exemption covers only licenses "issued before" enactment. It does not address pending applications, renewals, amendments, or expansions of existing licenses.

15. **§3(c), "environmental assessment" exemption:** The term is undefined, and the exemption has no volume cap, duration limit, required plan, permit, or reporting requirement. It also does not prohibit selling minerals recovered for assessment purposes. A purpose-based test is very hard to disprove, so this is the broadest gap in the bill.

**Section 4 (Registry)**

16. **§4(a), "operator" is undefined:** The bill does not say who must register (owner, charterer, operator, or manager). It also sets no registration deadline and no content requirements.

17. **§4(b), reports have no content standard:** The quarterly report must "describe" recovery activities, but the bill does not require volumes, locations, depths, or tonnage. It sets no deadline, no public-availability requirement, and no definition of "certified."

18. **§4 generally, no enforcement mechanism:** §5(a) penalizes only violations of §3. Failing to register or filing a false or missing report carries no civil penalty, so the registry is effectively voluntary.

19. **§4, no inspection or audit authority:** The bill gives NOAA no power to inspect vessels, examine records, issue subpoenas, or verify reports. Without that authority, the reporting requirement cannot be checked.

**Section 5 (Penalties)**

20. **§5 generally, no enforcing agency:** The bill does not say who brings civil or criminal actions (the Attorney General, NOAA, or another agency). It has no administrative penalty process, no injunctive-relief language, and no vessel seizure or forfeiture provision.

21. **§5(a), "each day" is undefined:** It is unclear whether a continuing operation counts as one violation per day, per vessel, per voyage, or per ton. The $1,000,000 maximum is also not inflation-adjusted and could be argued to be a cost of doing business.

22. **§5(a) vs. §8, conflicting start dates:** §5(a) applies to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but §8 delays the whole Act's effective date by 180 days. This creates an argument about whether conduct in the 180-day window is penalizable.

23. **§5(b), "willfully" is undefined:** The bill does not say what willfulness means for a corporate defendant or whether knowledge of the law is required. It also does not impose liability on officers or directors who direct the violation.

24. **§5, no liability for facilitators:** The bill penalizes only "any person who violates section 3." It does not reach aiding, abetting, financing, conspiracy, or directing a violation. It also does not address false statements in §4 reports.

25. **§5, limitations period not stated:** The bill does not set a statute of limitations and relies on default periods. Counsel should confirm the applicable periods under 28 U.S.C. §2462 and 18 U.S.C. §3282.

**Section 6 (International Agreement)**

26. **§6, "shall seek to negotiate" creates no obligation to succeed:** The Secretary must try but has no duty to reach an agreement, report to Congress, or face consequences for failing. The 18-month deadline is not enforceable in any practical sense.

27. **§6, "equivalent" is undefined, and treaty status is unclear:** The bill does not define what counts as an "equivalent" prohibition. It also does not say whether a future agreement would override the Act or require implementing legislation.

**Section 7 (Duration)**

28. **§7(a) vs. §7(b), internal conflict:** §7(a) keeps the prohibition in place until a joint resolution is enacted, but §7(b) ends the entire Act after 10 years regardless. The "indefinite" prohibition is therefore capped at about 10 years unless Congress extends the sunset.

29. **§7(a), "serious harm" is undefined:** The standard for lifting the prohibition is not defined. The bill also sets no deadline for the NASEM report and does not state what the report must address.

30. **§7(a), joint resolution procedure:** The bill does not say whether the resolution is subject to presentment to the President or what happens if it is vetoed. A resolution with legal effect that skips bicameralism and presentment could be challenged under *INS v. Chadha* (verify with counsel).

31. **§7(b), no savings clause:** The bill does not say what happens to accrued penalties, pending enforcement actions, or permits and obligations after the sunset. The sunset also runs from enactment rather than the effective date, leaving roughly 9.5 years of operation.

**Section 8 and General Provisions**

32. **§8, transition rules missing:** The 180-day delay applies to the whole Act, but the bill includes no transition rules for licenses, pending applications, or operations in progress. Sections 3(b), 5(a), 6, and 7(b) run from enactment, so the timing of obligations is inconsistent.

33. **No severability clause:** If a court strikes a provision (for example, the §2(1)(B) delegation or the §7(a) mechanism), the bill gives no guidance on whether the remaining prohibition survives. This invites challenges to the whole Act.

34. **No relationship to existing law:** The bill does not mention DSHMRA (30 U.S.C. §1401 et seq.), which already provides NOAA licensing and permitting for deep seabed hard mineral recovery. There is no conflict clause, savings clause, or "notwithstanding" language, so existing permits or DSHMRA's permit-issuance authority could be argued to survive.

35. **No rulemaking authority:** No agency is authorized to issue regulations, forms, or definitions. Key terms such as tonnage measurement, registry forms, and environmental assessment standards would remain undefined, and implementation would rest on agency discretion.

**Suggested priorities for the markup**

- **Most useful to us if left alone:** §3(c) (environmental assessment), §3(b) (no limits on grandfathered operations), §2(1)(A) (single-vessel trigger), and §2(2) (narrow U.S. person definition). These are the gaps that would let operations continue, and sponsors may not fix them quickly.
- **Most likely to be fixed by sponsors:** §5(a) (no penalty for registry violations), §7(a)/(b) (the sunset conflict), and §8 (effective-date inconsistency). Expect these to be corrected at or before markup, so decide early whether to raise them publicly.
- **Strongest for opposition arguments on challengeability:** §2(1)(B) (unbounded Secretary determination), §7(a) (joint resolution procedure and undefined "serious harm"), §6 (no enforceable obligation), and the missing DSHMRA conflict clause.

Before the Thursday markup, confirm the committee's deadline for filing amendments, since staff-prepared language often needs to be submitted in advance.
